prompt.context: I have just been talking with Rick Wagoner, GM's CEO, about his company's skyrocketing health care costs. GM pays for the health care of about 1.1M families, which equates to about $8-9B or $1500 per car sold. After a while, he began discussing the United States' healthcare problem on a national level. The US spends 15% of its GDP on health care while Japan spends 7-8% and Germany spends 10%. However, he says there is no evidence that health care is better in the US: average life expectancy is actually decreasing and about 45M people are uninsured. He wanted me to explore possible causes and solutions for the increasing cost trend with decreasing effectiveness/quality. He made a point of saying he didn't want to discuss politics, and shied away from fancy frameworks in our discussion.
prompt.question: Might you help me think about what to tell him? Specifically, what are the possible causes and solutions for the US healthcare system's increasing costs and decreasing effectiveness/quality?

clarifying_info.q: Is there any additional data or information available?
clarifying_info.a: There is no additional information to provide. The purpose of this case is to test poise and pressured thought.

clarifying_info.q: Should we focus on supply-side or demand-side factors?
clarifying_info.a: You may explore both supply and demand dimensions — the interviewer will follow your lead.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any constraints on the solutions we can propose?
clarifying_info.a: He made a point of saying he didn't want to discuss politics, so try to keep the discussion grounded in economic and structural analysis.

framework: Structure the analysis around Supply and Demand drivers of cost and quality
Demand side: behaviors and incentives that drive overuse or misuse of healthcare
Supply side: structural and market factors among providers, insurers, and pharma that inflate costs
For each driver, identify a corresponding solution and discuss trade-offs
Synthesize into a recommendation that addresses the most impactful levers

questions.prompt: Walk through the demand-side drivers of high US healthcare costs and declining quality.
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: (1) Lack of proactive/preventive care — people forgo preventive measures (nutrition, exercise, no-smoking) leading to expensive downstream complications like heart disease and diabetes; government or employer-sponsored prevention programs could shift incentives but financial return needs discussion. (2) Lack of healthcare for lower class — the US treats every ER patient regardless of insurance, which is far more expensive than early-intervention care; providing adequate care before problems become emergencies could reduce costs, but free-rider and socialization concerns arise.

questions.prompt: Walk through the supply-side drivers of high US healthcare costs and declining quality.
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: (1) Doctors' ability to induce demand — in over-saturated areas, doctors may order unnecessary tests to generate revenue; a fee-per-patient rather than fee-per-service model could address this, though practicality should be challenged. (2) Higher drug costs in the USA — the US subsidizes global drug consumption by paying higher prices, funding the majority of R&D and risk-premium costs for pharma; solutions include persuading drug companies to price uniformly globally or threatening reimportation, but long-term R&D implications must be discussed. (3) Emerging modular/boutique care — wealthy patients seek specialized private centers that only offer high-margin procedures (e.g., heart surgery), pulling funds from full-service facilities burdened by low-margin necessary services like ERs; regulatory responses or risks to full-service hospital viability should be discussed. (4) Profit motive — healthcare providers have invested in careers, R&D, and capital and seek returns; this creates incentives to manage rather than cure disease to maximize long-term cash flow rather than provide one-time treatment; socialization vs. current model trade-offs should be discussed.

questions.prompt: If the interviewer challenges your assertion — e.g., on privatized vs. socialized medicine — how do you defend or adjust your position?
questions.guidance: This case is explicitly designed to test poise under pressure. The interviewer will play devil's advocate on topics such as: privatized vs. socialized medicine, subsidized vs. unsubsidized medicine development/sales, healthcare availability for all, boutique hospitals vs. full-service hospitals, preventative vs. reactionary medicine. A strong candidate acknowledges the complexity, presents both sides with evidence or logic, and holds a reasoned position without becoming defensive or reversing under pressure without justification.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the structural causes — on both supply and demand sides — of the US healthcare cost and quality problem, and what solutions exist for each?

categories.name: Demand: Prevention and Lifestyle
ideas: Lack of nutritional planning, exercise, and anti-smoking programs leads to expensive chronic disease downstream
Government or employer-sponsored wellness programs could shift incentives
Financial return from prevention is diffuse and long-term, reducing private investment

categories.name: Demand: Access for Lower Income
ideas: Uninsured lower-class patients delay care until ER stage, which is far more expensive
Providing basic primary care before emergencies arise would reduce total system costs
Free-rider concerns and debates about socialization of medicine arise

categories.name: Supply: Physician Incentive Structures
ideas: Fee-for-service model allows doctors to induce demand with unnecessary tests in oversupplied markets
Fee-per-patient model would reduce unnecessary procedures
Practicality challenges: how to set appropriate capitation rates, quality monitoring

categories.name: Supply: Pharmaceutical Pricing
ideas: US consumers pay premium prices that subsidize global R&D costs
Uniform global pricing or reimportation threats could reduce US prices
Risk: reduced R&D investment could slow new drug development globally

categories.name: Supply: Boutique and Modular Care
ideas: High-margin specialized clinics (heart surgery, elective procedures) attract talent and capital away from full-service hospitals
Full-service hospitals lose cross-subsidy revenue and struggle with low-margin necessary services
Regulation of specialty-only facilities may be needed to preserve full-service capacity

categories.name: Supply: Profit Motive and Disease Management
ideas: All healthcare players earn more from chronic disease management than one-time cures
Incentive structure favors managing disease rather than curing it
Socialized models shift incentives toward prevention and cure but reduce private investment and innovation

recommendation: The US healthcare cost problem is driven by misaligned incentives on both supply and demand sides — the system currently rewards treatment over prevention, and high-volume/high-margin services over comprehensive access

The highest-impact levers are: shifting physician reimbursement from fee-for-service to fee-per-patient, investing in preventive care programs (especially employer- and government-sponsored), and addressing drug pricing through international negotiation or reimportation policy
Full-service hospital viability and long-term R&D investment must be protected in any reform approach
risks: Socialization of medicine may reduce innovation and private investment
Fee-per-patient models are difficult to calibrate and may underserve complex cases
Uniform drug pricing globally could reduce pharma R&D spending and slow new drug development
Removing profit motive may reduce quality and efficiency in delivery
next_steps: Quantify cost savings potential of shifting preventive care investment vs. ER-reactive spending
Model impact of fee-per-patient reimbursement on physician practice viability
Engage pharmaceutical industry on pricing negotiation feasibility
Assess regulatory frameworks for specialty clinic proliferation
